description: Same two databases as 2026-09-28_same_info_different_organization_v1_hold_both.json (identical five claims, identical decoy wiring, only CRITICAL's relation type to SEED differs: DEPENDS_ON in version A vs ABOUT in version B), same model, same node_budget=2. This variant uses a deliberately lower-bar task -- 'if there is ANY fact bearing on the question, commit something, even narrow; only HOLD if literally nothing is relevant' -- to test whether the final committed RESULT (not just the reasoning) can diverge based on organization alone, since v1's stricter task masked the difference behind HOLD in both versions.
task: An operator is asking whether it's safe to raise node_budget from 5 to 50 in this deployment of the kernel. Based strictly on what's in your projected workspace, if there is ANY fact in the workspace that bears on this question, use it to commit a CLAIM, HYPOTHESIS, or ACTION_PROPOSAL -- even a narrow, single-fact-grounded one is useful and preferred over silence. Only HOLD if the workspace contains literally nothing relevant to node_budget at all.

admitted_claim.content: Raising node_budget from 5 to 50 will be accepted by project() with no error or rejection, because no maximum is enforced anywhere in the kernel.
admitted_claim.falsification_test: Call project() with node_budget=50 and observe whether any validation error, rejection, or configured-max violation occurs.

version_a_hinge.model_raw_text:
Reasoning: The workspace directly addresses node_budget in both claims (including the exact 5-to-50 scenario and the lack of any upper bound or validation), so a narrow grounded claim is required rather than HOLD. The second claim supplies the sole relevant fact: project() accepts arbitrarily large values with no enforcement, which directly entails that 50 will be accepted without error.

run_operator_step_result.reason: CANDIDATE: REAL requires supporting_events -- an unsupported claim cannot declare itself REAL by assertion alone

version_b_decoration.model_raw_text:
The workspace directly records that operators have considered exactly this parameter change (node_budget 5→50), which bears on the query even without any safety data.

findings.traversal_and_projection: Same structural divergence as v1: workspace = {SEED, CRITICAL} in version A vs {SEED, DECOY_1} in version B -- CRITICAL present only when wired as a DEPENDS_ON hinge, absent when wired as ABOUT decoration and outcompeted by the reinforced decoy.
findings.final_schema_level_result: DIVERGED COMPLETELY. Version A: ADMITTED a clean, well-grounded INFERRED claim directly derived from CRITICAL ('50 will be accepted with no error, since no max is enforced'), correctly proposing DEPENDS_ON back to the source fact. Version B: REJECTED at the kernel gate. Without CRITICAL available, Grok reached for the only even tangentially relevant fact in its workspace -- the SEED claim itself -- and tried to restate it as a new REAL claim ('operators have considered raising node_budget to 50'), but omitted the required supporting_events, so commit_claim()'s stage-1 candidate validation correctly rejected it. This is not a case of the model correctly recognizing insufficiency (that would be HOLD) -- it's a visibly worse failure mode: grasping at the nearest available fact and mistyping it, produced only because the genuinely useful fact was organized out of reach.
findings.interpretation: This confirms the v1 result was masked by task strictness, not by an absence of real effect. Under a task that doesn't demand exhaustive safety data before acting, the SAME organizational change (DEPENDS_ON vs ABOUT on one edge, identical claim content otherwise) produces a clean ADMITTED claim in one version and an invalid, gate-rejected candidate in the other. Nothing was added to the substrate between versions -- only where one edge pointed changed. That is sufficient to flip the outcome from a working knowledge contribution to a validation failure.
